decks.title: Business Environment — Part 1: Meaning, Features, Importance and Scanning
goals: Explain the meaning and features of business environment
Discuss how understanding the environment helps a firm spot opportunities and threats early
Define environmental scanning and explain why firms monitor their environment continuously

slides.heading: Business Environment
slides.body_md: Part 1: what the **business environment** is, its **features**, why it **matters**, and how firms **scan** it.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: the meaning of business environment, its features, its importance and environmental scanning
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: No business works in a vacuum. Suppliers raise prices, customers change their minds, rivals cut rates, and governments pass new laws. All these forces together make up the business environment. In this part we see what it is, what it is like, why a firm must understand it, and how firms keep watch on it.

slides.heading: What is business environment?
slides.body_md: **Business environment** is the sum total of all **individuals, institutions and forces**, internal and external, that affect the working and performance of a firm.

The firm's control falls as we move outwards
visual.caption: The firm sits inside its micro environment, which sits inside the macro environment.

slides.narration: Picture the firm at the centre. Close to it are its own internal factors, such as its mission, people and money. Around these are suppliers, customers, competitors and others it deals with directly. Outermost are the big economic, social, technological, political and legal forces. The further out a force is, the less the firm can control it.

slides.heading: Features of business environment

rows: All forces, taken together, form the environment
Some affect one firm (a rival next door); some affect all (a tax change)
A change in one factor sets off changes in others
Future changes are hard to predict
Many factors act together, so effects are hard to judge
Its impact differs by place and firm

visual.alt: Table of seven features of business environment with their meanings

slides.narration: The environment has seven features. It is a totality of forces. Some forces are specific, touching one firm, and some are general, touching all. The forces are inter-related. The environment is dynamic, always changing, and therefore uncertain. Because many forces act together it is complex, and because its effect differs from place to place it is relative.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: which feature?
slides.body_md: Match each imagined situation with the feature it shows.
bullets: Step 1: look for the **clue**: place, a chain of changes, prediction, or one firm versus all.
Step 2: name the feature.
Step 3: explain in one line.

rows: Woollen jackets sell in Shimla, not in Chennai
Fuel prices rise, buyers want e-scooters, mechanics retrain
Festival colours for next year cannot be predicted
A rival opens next door; the government changes a tax

visual.alt: Worked table matching four imagined situations with the feature of business environment each shows
visual.caption: Find the clue word: place, chain of changes, prediction, or one firm versus all firms.

slides.narration: Let us practise. Jackets selling in Shimla but not in Chennai show relativity, because the effect depends on the place. Fuel prices leading to electric scooters and then to retrained mechanics show inter-relatedness. Not knowing next year's colours shows uncertainty. A rival next door is a specific force, while a tax change is a general one.

slides.heading: Quick check: complexity
slides.body_md: True or false: the environment is simple because each factor acts on its own.
slides.narration: Think about whether factors act alone or together.

slides.heading: Why the environment matters

rows: Pahadi Organics launches millet snacks a year before rivals
Tamarind Tiffins starts phone ordering when cloud kitchens open
A firm learns of a cheaper input supplier or a bank scheme
A workshop retrains mechanics for electric scooters
A tea estate times its exports with demand forecasts
Firms that read change early keep customers and margins

visual.alt: Table of six benefits of understanding the business environment, each with an imagined example

slides.narration: Understanding the environment helps a firm in six ways. It spots opportunities early and gains a first-mover advantage. It gets early warning of threats. It finds useful resources such as finance and inputs. It copes with rapid change. It plans better. And all of this improves its performance.

slides.heading: Opportunity or threat?
columns:
**Opportunity**

A favourable change the firm can use, such as rising demand for millet snacks.

**Threat**

A change that can harm the firm, such as new rivals with app ordering.

rows: An opportunity for a health-food firm
A threat to a lunch-box service

visual.alt: Table of two imagined changes, one an opportunity and one a threat

slides.narration: The same change can be an opportunity for one firm and a threat for another. A craze for millet snacks helps a health-food maker but may hurt a fried-snack seller. That is why each firm must read the environment in the light of its own business.

slides.heading: Quick check: uncertainty
slides.body_md: A garment exporter cannot be sure which festival colours will sell next year. Which feature is this?
slides.narration: Ask whether the future can be predicted with confidence.

slides.heading: Environmental scanning
slides.body_md: **Environmental scanning** is the continuous gathering and analysis of information about the environment to detect **early signals** of opportunities and threats.

visual.alt: Flow of environmental scanning: gather information, analyse the signals, share them with managers, plan a response, and keep watching
visual.caption: Scanning is a continuous cycle.

slides.narration: Scanning is how a firm keeps its eyes open. It gathers information from news, trade fairs, customers and rivals. It analyses the signals, shares them with managers, and plans a response. Then it keeps watching, because the environment never stops changing. Scanning is a cycle, not a one-time task.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a scanning log
slides.body_md: An imagined marble-craft firm in Jodhpur keeps a monthly log of signals.
bullets: Step 1: note the signal.
Step 2: decide whether it is an **opportunity** or a **threat**.
Step 3: plan a response.

rows: Export portal waives fees for artisans

visual.alt: Worked scanning log of an imagined marble-craft firm: three signals classified as opportunity or threat with a planned response
visual.caption: Imagined scanning log of Aravalli Stone Crafts, Jodhpur.

slides.narration: Here is an imagined scanning log. Hotels asking for eco-friendly décor is an opportunity, so the firm designs a light range. Cheap resin copies online are a threat, so it stresses hand carving. An export portal waiving fees is an opportunity, so it lists its products there. Each signal leads to an action.

slides.heading: Quick check: scanning
slides.body_md: Fill in the blank: careful monitoring of the environment for early signals is environmental ___.
slides.narration: One word completes the name of this process.

slides.heading: Who scans, and how often?

rows: Top managers lead; every manager contributes
News, trade fairs, customers, suppliers, rivals, government notices
To act before rivals and avoid surprises

visual.alt: Table answering who scans the environment, from which sources, how often and why

slides.narration: Scanning is led by top managers, but every manager notices something useful, from a salesperson's talk with a customer to a buyer's chat with a supplier. Firms review these signals regularly, so that they can act before their rivals and are not caught by surprise.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: All forces, inside and outside, that affect a firm
Totality, specific and general, inter-related, dynamic, uncertain, complex, relative
Opportunities, threats, resources, change, planning, performance
Continuous monitoring to catch early signals

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: meaning, features, importance and environmental scanning

slides.narration: To sum up Part 1. The business environment is the total of all forces, inside and outside, that affect a firm. It is complex, dynamic, uncertain, inter-related and relative. Understanding it helps a firm seize opportunities, prepare for threats and plan better. Firms keep track of it through continuous environmental scanning.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Learn the **definition** word for word: individuals, institutions and forces.
For features, find the **clue** in the case.
For importance, link each point to the **firm in the question**.
Scanning is **continuous**: never say it is done once.

visual.alt: Three steps for case questions: quote the line, name the factor or dimension, and explain its effect

slides.narration: A few tips. Use the full definition with individuals, institutions and forces. In feature questions, spot the clue in the case. In importance questions, tie each point to the firm you are given. And remember that scanning is continuous. In every case question, quote the line, name the idea and explain it.

decks.title: Business Environment — Part 2: Micro and Macro Environment and SWOT
goals: Identify internal factors and external micro factors of a firm's environment
Classify changes into economic, social, technological, political and legal dimensions and explain their effects
Prepare a simple SWOT analysis for a small Indian business

slides.heading: Micro, Macro and SWOT
slides.body_md: Part 2: the **internal** factors, the **external micro** factors, the five **macro** dimensions, and **SWOT** analysis.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: internal factors, external micro factors, the five macro dimensions and SWOT analysis
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In Part 2 we open up the layers of the environment. First, the factors inside the firm. Then the people and firms it deals with directly. Then the big forces that shape every business. Finally, we bring them together in a simple tool called SWOT analysis.

slides.heading: Internal factors
slides.body_md: Internal factors lie **inside** the firm and are largely **within its control**.

rows: A firm that refuses to use child labour
A trusted brand, a dealer network

visual.alt: Table of internal factors of the environment with examples

slides.narration: Internal factors include the firm's values, mission and objectives, its structure and culture, its people, its machines and technology, its money, and its brand and marketing strength. Because they are inside the firm, managers can change them, though not overnight.

slides.heading: External micro factors
slides.body_md: External micro factors are the people and firms the business deals with **directly**.

visual.alt: Table of six external micro factors, who they are and how each affects a firm

slides.narration: Outside the firm but close to it are six groups. Suppliers sell it inputs. Customers buy its products. Competitors sell similar products. Marketing intermediaries, such as dealers and couriers, help its goods reach buyers. Financiers lend it money. And the public, including media and local residents, shapes its image.

slides.heading: Quick check: inside or outside?
slides.body_md: Which of these is an internal factor of the micro environment?
slides.narration: Look for the factor that the firm itself decides.

slides.heading: Micro versus macro
columns:
**Micro environment**

Immediate surroundings; affects one firm directly; some factors can be influenced.

**Macro environment**

Wider forces; affect all firms; beyond the firm's control.

visual.alt: Table comparing micro and macro environment on nearness, effect and control

slides.narration: The micro environment is close to the firm and affects it directly; a firm can bargain with suppliers or win over customers. The macro environment is wider. It shapes every firm in the economy, and no single firm can control it.

slides.heading: The macro environment

rows: Interest rates, inflation, incomes, economic policy
More working couples buy meal kits
Salt and sugar must be shown on packs

visual.alt: Table of the five macro dimensions, what each includes and an imagined change for each

slides.narration: The macro environment has five dimensions. Economic covers interest rates, inflation, incomes and economic policy. Social covers values, habits and lifestyles. Technological covers new methods and machines. Political covers stability and the government's attitude to business. Legal covers the laws and rules a firm must follow.

slides.heading: Economic policy changes since 1991

rows: Fewer licences and controls; freer business decisions
Smaller role for the public sector
Closer links with the world economy through trade, investment and technology

visual.alt: Table of liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation with their meanings

slides.narration: Since nineteen ninety one, Indian business has worked in a very different economic environment. Liberalisation removed many licences and controls. Privatisation reduced the role of the public sector. Globalisation linked India more closely with the world through trade, investment and technology.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: classifying changes
slides.body_md: An imagined bakery in Indore faces four changes.
bullets: Step 1: ask whether the change is about **money, people, machines, government or law**.
Step 2: name the dimension.
Step 3: state one effect.

rows: A new oven controls baking by app

visual.alt: Worked table classifying four changes faced by an imagined bakery into macro dimensions with their effects
visual.caption: Ask: is it about money, people, machines, government or law?

slides.narration: Let us classify four changes for an imagined bakery. A labelling law is legal, so packs must be redesigned. Rising wheat prices are economic, so costs go up. Buyers wanting whole-grain bread is social, so new lines are needed. An oven controlled by an app is technological, giving steadier quality.

slides.heading: Quick check: odd one out
slides.body_md: Which one is **not** part of the macro environment?
slides.narration: One option affects only firms in the same market. Which one?

slides.heading: SWOT analysis
slides.body_md: **SWOT** studies a firm's internal **Strengths** and **Weaknesses**, and the external **Opportunities** and **Threats** it faces.

slides.narration: SWOT brings everything together. The top row looks inside the firm: strengths, what it does well, and weaknesses, what holds it back. The bottom row looks outside: opportunities, favourable changes it can use, and threats, harmful changes it must guard against.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a simple SWOT
slides.body_md: Facts about an imagined lunch-box service in Madurai: loyal office customers; only two delivery staff; offices back to full attendance; cloud kitchens nearby.
bullets: Step 1: sort facts into **inside** and **outside**.
Step 2: mark each as **helpful** or **harmful**.
Step 3: fill the four boxes.

visual.alt: Worked SWOT table for an imagined lunch-box service: loyal customers as a strength, few delivery staff as a weakness, offices returning as an opportunity, cloud kitchens as a threat
visual.caption: Imagined SWOT of Tamarind Tiffins, Madurai.

slides.narration: Sort the facts. Loyal customers are inside and helpful, a strength. Only two delivery staff are inside and harmful, a weakness. Offices returning to full attendance are outside and helpful, an opportunity. Cloud kitchens nearby are outside and harmful, a threat. A good plan uses strengths to grab opportunities.

slides.heading: Quick check: a threat
slides.body_md: A supermarket chain plans a bakery section in the same market as a small bakery. In the small bakery's SWOT, this is…
slides.narration: Is it inside or outside the bakery, and does it help or harm?

slides.heading: Summary of Part 2

rows: Mission, values, structure, culture, people, money, technology, image
Suppliers, customers, competitors, intermediaries, financiers, public
Strengths and weaknesses inside; opportunities and threats outside

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 2: internal factors, external micro factors, macro dimensions and SWOT

slides.narration: To sum up Part 2. Internal factors such as mission, people and money are largely controllable. External micro factors are suppliers, customers, competitors, intermediaries, financiers and the public. The macro environment has economic, social, technological, political and legal dimensions. SWOT sorts strengths and weaknesses inside the firm from opportunities and threats outside.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Name the **exact** micro factor: supplier, intermediary, financier or public.
Classify macro changes by asking **money, people, machines, government or law**.
In SWOT, **S and W are internal**, **O and T are external**.
Link each SWOT point to a **fact in the case**.

visual.alt: Three steps for case questions: quote the line, name the factor or dimension, and explain its effect

slides.narration: Final tips. Name micro factors precisely; a courier is an intermediary, a bank is a financier. Classify macro changes with the simple question: money, people, machines, government or law. In SWOT, keep strengths and weaknesses inside and opportunities and threats outside. And always tie your points to the facts given.

notes.title: Business Environment — notes

sections.heading: 1. Meaning and features of business environment
sections.body_md:
**Business environment** is the sum total of all **individuals, institutions and forces**, internal and external, that affect the working and performance of a business.

**Features:**
- **Totality of forces:** the environment is the sum of all forces, taken together.
- **Specific and general forces:** specific forces (suppliers, customers, competitors) affect a particular firm directly; general forces (economic, social, political, legal, technological) affect all firms.
- **Inter-relatedness:** factors are linked, so a change in one leads to changes in others.
- **Dynamic:** the environment keeps changing.
- **Uncertainty:** future changes are difficult to predict.
- **Complexity:** many factors act together, so their combined effect is hard to judge.
- **Relativity:** its impact differs from country to country, region to region and firm to firm.

key_terms.definition_md: All individuals, institutions and forces, internal and external, that affect a business.
Forces such as suppliers and competitors that affect a particular firm directly.
Forces such as economic policy and laws that affect all firms.

sections.heading: 2. Importance of understanding the environment
sections.body_md:
- **Identifying opportunities and getting the first-mover advantage:** firms that spot a favourable trend early can enter before rivals.
- **Early warning signals of threats:** knowing about possible dangers in time lets a firm prepare.
- **Tapping useful resources:** the environment is a source of inputs, finance and skills.
- **Coping with rapid changes:** firms that watch the environment adapt faster.
- **Assisting in planning and policy formulation:** knowledge of the environment is the basis of plans.
- **Improving performance:** firms that read the environment well tend to do better over time.

The same change can be an **opportunity** for one firm and a **threat** for another.

key_terms.definition_md: The benefit of being first to use an opportunity, before rivals.

rows: Pahadi Organics launches millet snacks a year before rivals
Tamarind Tiffins starts phone ordering when cloud kitchens open
A firm learns of a cheaper input supplier or a bank scheme
A workshop retrains mechanics for electric scooters
A tea estate times its exports with demand forecasts
Firms that read change early keep customers and margins

visual.alt: Table of six benefits of understanding the business environment, each with an imagined example

sections.heading: 3. Environmental scanning
sections.body_md:
**Environmental scanning** is the careful, **continuous** monitoring of the internal and external environment — gathering, analysing and passing on information about events, trends and relationships — to detect **early signals** of opportunities and threats.

**Why firms scan:** the environment is dynamic and uncertain; early information lets a firm plan, avoid surprises and act before rivals.

**How:** gather information (news, trade fairs, customers, suppliers, rivals, government notices) → analyse it into opportunities and threats → share it with managers → plan a response → keep watching.

key_terms.definition_md: Continuous monitoring of the environment to detect early signals of change.

visual.alt: Flow of environmental scanning: gather information, analyse the signals, share them with managers, plan a response, and keep watching
visual.caption: Scanning is a continuous cycle.

rows: Export portal waives fees for artisans

visuals.caption: Imagined scanning log of Aravalli Stone Crafts, Jodhpur.

sections.heading: 4. The micro environment
sections.body_md:
**Internal factors** (largely controllable): value system; vision, mission and objectives; management structure and internal relationships; corporate culture; human resources; physical resources and technological capability; financial resources; marketing resources; company image and brand equity.

**External micro factors** (the firm's immediate surroundings):
- **Suppliers** — sellers of raw materials and components.
- **Customers** — individuals, businesses, government, exporters who buy the product.
- **Competitors** — firms offering similar or substitute products.
- **Marketing intermediaries** — dealers, wholesalers, retailers, couriers, online platforms, advertising agencies.
- **Financiers** — banks and other lenders and investors.
- **Public** — media, local residents, citizens' groups and others with an interest in the firm.

key_terms.definition_md: Factors inside the firm, largely within its control.
Firms that help a business promote, sell and distribute its goods.
Any group with an actual or potential interest in, or effect on, the firm.

rows: A firm that refuses to use child labour
A trusted brand, a dealer network

visuals.alt: Table of six external micro factors, who they are and how each affects a firm

sections.heading: 5. The macro environment
sections.body_md:
- **Economic:** interest rates, inflation, incomes, savings, stock-market conditions, economic policies (since 1991: **liberalisation**, **privatisation**, **globalisation**).
- **Social:** customs, traditions, values, habits, lifestyles, education, population trends.
- **Technological:** new methods, machines, products and innovations (digital payments, e-commerce, automation).
- **Political:** political stability, the government's attitude to business, relations with other countries.
- **Legal:** laws and rules — for example on companies, competition, consumer protection, taxes and labelling.

Macro forces affect **all** firms and are **beyond** the control of any single firm.

Reducing the role of the public sector.
Integrating the economy with the world economy.

sections.heading: 6. SWOT analysis
sections.body_md:
**SWOT analysis** examines a firm's **Strengths** and **Weaknesses** (internal) and the **Opportunities** and **Threats** (external) it faces.

**Preparing a simple SWOT:** list the facts; sort them into inside and outside; mark each as helpful or harmful; fill the four boxes.

**Using it:** build on strengths, correct weaknesses, grab opportunities, and guard against threats — ideally using a strength to seize an opportunity.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Calling customers or suppliers internal factors (they are external micro factors).
- Mixing up a firm's own weakness with an outside threat in SWOT.
- Saying environmental scanning is done once.
- Classifying consumer tastes as technological (they are social).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: one correct option, factor or dimension.
- 2–3 marks: each point named and explained, linked to the case.
- 5 marks: parts answered separately; SWOT with all four boxes; macro answers with an example for each dimension.
- Case questions: quote the line, name the factor, explain its effect.

questions.stem_md: Which statement best describes the **business environment** of a firm?

options.text_md: Only the government rules that a firm must obey
The sum total of all individuals, institutions and forces, inside and outside the firm, that affect its working and performance
The physical surroundings of a factory, such as air and water
The list of customers who buy from the firm

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The sum total of all individuals, institutions and forces, inside and outside the firm, that affect its working and performance. Business environment is the totality of forces and institutions, internal and external, that influence a business. Laws, natural surroundings or customers are only parts of it.

questions.stem_md: Chinar Woollens, an imagined shawl maker in Srinagar, faces two changes: a rival opens a showroom on the same street, and the government changes the tax rate on all textiles. These two changes are examples of, respectively,

options.text_md: a general force and a specific force
a specific force and a general force

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** a specific force and a general force. A rival on the same street affects this firm directly (specific force); a tax change for all textiles affects every firm in the industry (general force).

questions.stem_md: Rising petrol prices made commuters in an imagined town prefer electric scooters, which in turn led a local workshop to train its mechanics in battery repair. Which feature of business environment does this chain of changes show best?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Inter-relatedness. A change in one factor (economic: fuel prices) set off changes in others (social: commuter preference; technological: new repair skills). The factors are inter-related.

questions.stem_md: Fashion trends for festival wear can change within a single season, so a garment exporter cannot be sure which colours will sell next year. This illustrates that the business environment is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** uncertain. Future changes in the environment are difficult to predict, especially in fast-moving areas such as fashion and technology: uncertainty.

questions.stem_md: Thick woollen jackets sell briskly in Shimla but hardly at all in Chennai, although they are made by the same imagined firm. Which feature of business environment explains this?

options.text_md: Relativity: the environment differs from place to place

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Relativity: the environment differs from place to place. The impact of environmental factors differs from country to country and region to region (here, climate and local needs): relativity.

questions.stem_md: Pahadi Organics, an imagined food firm in Almora, noticed early that health-conscious buyers were asking for millet snacks and launched a range a year before its rivals, capturing most of the shelf space. Which benefit of understanding the environment does this show?

options.text_md: It helps the firm identify opportunities and gain a first-mover advantage
It helps the firm identify threats and give early warning
It helps the firm tap useful resources
It helps the firm improve its internal culture

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** It helps the firm identify opportunities and gain a first-mover advantage. By spotting a positive trend early, the firm got there first. Identifying opportunities brings a first-mover advantage.

questions.stem_md: Tamarind Tiffins, an imagined lunch-box service in Madurai, saw three cloud kitchens open nearby with app-based ordering. It quickly started its own phone ordering and loyalty card. Understanding the environment helped it mainly by

options.text_md: gaining a first-mover advantage in a new market
identifying a threat and acting on the early warning

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** identifying a threat and acting on the early warning. The cloud kitchens were a threat; noticing them early let the firm respond before losing customers.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The business environment is dynamic.

**Reason (R):** Technology, consumer tastes, laws and economic conditions keep changing over time.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and continuous change in its factors is exactly why the environment is called dynamic.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A firm can study and respond to its external environment.

**Reason (R):** A firm can fully control the factors of its external environment.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The assertion is true: firms monitor the environment and adapt. The reason is false: external factors such as government policy or competitors are largely beyond the firm's control.

questions.stem_md: The business environment is simple to understand because each of its factors acts on its own.
questions.solution_md: **False.** False. Many factors act together and affect one another, so the environment is complex and its combined effect is hard to judge.

questions.stem_md: Complete the analogy. A rival opening a shop next door : Specific force :: A change in interest rates by the Reserve Bank of India : ___
questions.solution_md: A rival next door affects one firm directly (specific force); an interest-rate change affects all firms alike, so it is a general force.

questions.stem_md: Explain any two features of business environment.
questions.solution_md: Any two features (totality, specific and general forces, inter-relatedness, dynamic, uncertainty, complexity, relativity), each explained.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Dynamic:** the environment keeps **changing** — technology, tastes and laws do not stay the same.
2. **Inter-related:** its factors **affect one another**; a change in fuel prices can alter buying habits and spur new technology.

questions.stem_md: Lohit Tea Estate, an imagined tea grower in Dibrugarh, tracks rainfall forecasts, export demand and new government schemes every month. State two ways in which this understanding helps the estate.
questions.solution_md: Two benefits (planning, opportunities, threats, resources, coping with change, performance) linked to the estate.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. It helps **plan and formulate policies**, for example timing plucking and exports with forecasts.
2. It helps **identify opportunities** such as new **government schemes** or rising export demand, and **threats** such as poor rainfall, before rivals do.

marking_scheme.step: First benefit linked to the case
Second benefit linked to the case

questions.stem_md: Coromandel Cocoa, an imagined chocolate maker in Kochi, studies its environment closely. Explain three ways in which this helps the firm, with an example of each from a chocolate business.
questions.solution_md: Any three benefits (opportunities, threats, resources, coping with change, planning, performance), each with a chocolate example.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Identifying opportunities:** noticing demand for **sugar-free chocolate** lets it launch early and gain a first-mover advantage.
2. **Early warning of threats:** seeing an imported brand cut prices lets it plan a **response** in time.
3. **Tapping resources:** knowing **cocoa growers' cooperatives** and banks helps it secure inputs and finance on good terms.

questions.stem_md: Explain the features of business environment that make it difficult for managers to predict its effects: uncertainty, complexity and relativity.
questions.solution_md: Each of the three features explained.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Uncertainty:** future changes are **hard to predict**, especially in fast-moving fields such as technology and fashion.
2. **Complexity:** many factors act **together** and affect one another, so their **combined** effect is hard to judge.
3. **Relativity:** the impact differs from **place to place** and firm to firm, so one firm's experience cannot simply be copied.

questions.stem_md:
(a) What is meant by business environment? [1]
(b) Explain any two features of business environment. [2]
(c) Zari Threads, an imagined maker of silk yarn in Varanasi, ignored reports that power looms were replacing handlooms and lost half its buyers in two years. Explain two ways in which studying the environment could have helped it. [2]
questions.solution_md: Meaning; two features; two benefits applied to Zari Threads.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Business environment** is the **sum total of all individuals, institutions and forces**, internal and external, that **affect the working and performance** of a firm.

(b) **Dynamic** — it keeps **changing** with technology, tastes and laws. **Uncertain** — future changes are **hard to predict**, so firms must keep watching it.

(c) **Early warning of threats:** regular study would have shown the **shift to power looms**, giving time to **adapt** its yarn for them. **Coping with rapid change:** knowing the trend early, the firm could have **retrained** staff and **found new buyers** instead of losing half its customers.

marking_scheme.step: (c) Two benefits applied to the case

questions.stem_md: Environmental scanning means

options.text_md: cleaning the surroundings of a factory to reduce pollution
continuously gathering and analysing information about the environment to detect early signs of opportunities and threats
checking the accounts of a firm at the end of the year
scanning products with bar codes at the billing counter

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** continuously gathering and analysing information about the environment to detect early signs of opportunities and threats. Environmental scanning is the careful monitoring of the environment, both internal and external, to spot early signals of change.

questions.stem_md: Officers of the imagined Narmada Dairy Cooperative in Jabalpur read trade magazines, visit food fairs, note the prices of rival brands and collect farmers' feedback every month, and then discuss what they found. This activity is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** environmental scanning. Regularly collecting and analysing information about the environment to spot signals of change is environmental scanning. SWOT may use these findings, but the activity described is scanning.

questions.stem_md: Why should environmental scanning be a continuous activity rather than a one-time exercise?

options.text_md: Because laws require firms to scan every day

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Because the environment keeps changing. The environment is dynamic, so information gathered once soon becomes out of date.

questions.stem_md: Environmental scanning needs to be done only once, when a business is first set up.
questions.solution_md: **False.** False. Because the environment is dynamic, scanning has to be continuous.

questions.stem_md: The careful monitoring of the environment to detect early signals of change is called environmental ___.
questions.solution_md: Environmental scanning.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Environmental scanning helps a firm spot opportunities and threats early.

**Reason (R):** The micro environment includes suppliers, customers and competitors.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both statements are true, but the make-up of the micro environment does not explain why scanning gives early signals; that comes from continuous monitoring of change.

questions.stem_md: What is environmental scanning? Give one reason why firms carry it out.
questions.solution_md: Meaning plus one reason.

answer.model_answer_md: **Environmental scanning** is the **continuous gathering and analysis of information** about the internal and external environment to **detect early signals** of change. Firms do it to **spot opportunities and threats in time** and plan their response.

questions.stem_md: Explain how Aravalli Stone Crafts, an imagined small firm making marble handicrafts in Jodhpur, could carry out environmental scanning, giving one example for each step: gathering, analysing and using the information.
questions.solution_md: Three steps of scanning, each with a suitable example.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Gathering:** the owner collects information from **trade fairs, export portals, newspapers and buyers' feedback**, for example on demand for light-weight décor.
2. **Analysing:** the team **sorts** the signals into **opportunities and threats**, for example rising online orders and cheaper resin copies.
3. **Using it:** the findings are **shared** with managers and used to **plan**, for example opening an online store.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is an **internal** factor in the micro environment of a firm?

options.text_md: The suppliers of its raw material
The customers who buy its products
The firm's own mission, objectives and value system
The banks that lend to it

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The firm's own mission, objectives and value system. Mission, objectives and values are inside the firm and largely under its control. Suppliers, customers and financiers are external micro factors.

questions.stem_md: Coromandel Cocoa (imagined) has to raise its chocolate prices because the cooperative that sells it cocoa beans has raised its rates by a fifth. Which factor of its environment caused the change?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Suppliers, an external micro factor. The cocoa cooperative supplies raw material; suppliers belong to the external micro environment.

questions.stem_md: Sundarban Honey, an imagined firm in Kolkata, sells through a network of distributors, a courier company and two online marketplaces. In its micro environment, these are
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** marketing intermediaries. Firms that help a business distribute, deliver and sell its goods are marketing intermediaries.

questions.stem_md: Residents of a colony near the imagined Malwa Bakes factory in Indore complain to the media about smoke from its ovens, and a local newspaper carries the story. Which part of the micro environment does this group represent?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Public (local public and media). Any group with an actual or potential interest in, or effect on, the firm — local residents, media, citizens' groups — is part of the public in the micro environment.

questions.stem_md: Half of the skilled carpenters of Shillong Bamboo Furniture, an imagined firm, left for better-paying jobs, and orders were delayed. The factor affected is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** human resources, an internal factor. The skills and number of a firm's own employees are an internal factor (human resources).

questions.stem_md: Two new brands of packaged idli batter started offering free delivery in the city where an imagined batter maker sells. Which external micro factor is the maker facing?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Competitors. Other firms selling similar products to the same buyers are competitors.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Customers are an internal factor of a firm's micro environment.

**Reason (R):** A firm can fully decide what its customers will buy.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Both statements are false. Customers are an external micro factor, and a firm can influence but not control their choices.

questions.stem_md: Internal factors of the environment, such as a firm's policies and resources, are generally within its control.
questions.solution_md: **True.** True. A firm can change its own policies, structure and resources, though not overnight; external factors are largely beyond its control.

questions.stem_md: Complete the analogy. A bank that lends money to the firm : Financier :: A wholesaler who stocks and resells the firm's goods : ___
questions.solution_md: A lending bank is a financier; a wholesaler who helps the goods reach buyers is a marketing intermediary.

questions.stem_md: Match each factor in the micro environment of an imagined spice exporter with its category.

options.text_md: Pepper growers who sell to the exporter
Foreign importers who buy its spices
A shipping agent who books containers

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Growers supply inputs; importers are customers; the value system is internal; the shipping agent helps deliver the goods, so it is an intermediary.

questions.stem_md: Explain any two internal factors of a firm's environment.
questions.solution_md: Any two internal factors (value system, mission and objectives, structure, culture, human, physical, technological, financial or marketing resources, image) explained.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Value system and mission:** the beliefs and goals of the owners shape **policies and choices**, such as a firm refusing to use child labour.
2. **Financial resources:** the **funds** available decide whether the firm can expand, buy technology or survive a bad year.

questions.stem_md: Kutch Salt Works, an imagined salt producer, sells through local wholesalers and depends on a transport firm for trucks. A rival has just cut prices. Identify two external micro factors in this situation and say how each affects the firm.
questions.solution_md: Two external micro factors identified from the case, each with its effect.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Marketing intermediaries** — the **wholesalers** and **transport firm** decide how fast and widely its salt reaches buyers.
2. **Competitors** — the **rival's price cut** may take away its customers, forcing it to respond.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between the micro environment and the macro environment of a business on any three bases.
questions.solution_md: Three valid bases of difference.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Nearness:** the micro environment is the firm's **immediate** surroundings; the macro environment is the **wider** setting.
2. **Components:** micro covers **internal factors, suppliers, customers, competitors, intermediaries, financiers and the public**; macro covers **economic, social, technological, political and legal** forces.
3. **Control and effect:** micro factors affect **one firm directly** and some can be influenced; macro forces affect **all firms** and are beyond the firm's control.

questions.stem_md: Shillong Bamboo Furniture (imagined) has a strong brand among hotels, an old machine shop, and owners who insist on using only certified bamboo. Identify three internal factors from these details and explain how each affects the firm.
questions.solution_md: Three internal factors drawn from the details, each with its effect.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Company image and brand:** the **strong brand among hotels** brings repeat orders and lets it charge a fair price.
2. **Physical assets and technology:** the **old machine shop** limits speed and finish, and may raise costs.
3. **Value system:** insisting on **certified bamboo** builds trust with eco-conscious buyers but may raise raw-material cost.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Distinguish between internal and external factors of a firm's environment. [1]
(b) Sahyadri EV Scooters, an imagined maker in Nashik, buys batteries from one supplier, sells through 40 dealers, borrows from a cooperative bank, and faces two bigger rival brands. Identify four external micro factors and explain how each could affect the firm. [4]
questions.solution_md: Distinction; four external micro factors with effects.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Internal factors** (such as policies, structure and resources) are **within the firm** and largely controllable; **external factors** (such as suppliers, customers, competitors, the economy and laws) are **outside** it and largely beyond its control.

(b) 1. **Supplier** — depending on **one battery supplier** means any delay or price rise stops production.
2. **Marketing intermediaries** — the **40 dealers** decide how widely and quickly scooters reach buyers.
3. **Financier** — the **cooperative bank's** terms decide how cheaply the firm can expand.
4. **Competitors** — the **two bigger rivals** may cut prices or launch new models, forcing Sahyadri to respond.

questions.stem_md: The Reserve Bank of India raises its policy rate, and banks increase interest on business loans. For an imagined furniture maker planning a new factory, this change belongs to the
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** economic environment. Interest rates, inflation, income and economic policies form the economic environment.

questions.stem_md: More working couples in an imagined city now prefer ready-to-cook meal kits to cooking from scratch. An imagined food firm sees this as a change in its
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** social environment. Changes in lifestyles, habits, values and family patterns are part of the social environment.

questions.stem_md: Farmers near an imagined pesticide dealer start hiring drones to spray crops, cutting spraying time by more than half. This is a change in the
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** technological environment. New methods, machines and innovations make up the technological environment.

questions.stem_md: An imagined foreign electronics company decides to build a plant in a state because the government there has been stable for years and welcomes investment. Which macro dimension most influenced its decision?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Political environment. Political stability and the government's attitude to business form the political environment.

questions.stem_md: A new rule requires all packaged snacks to show the amount of salt and sugar on the front of the pack, and an imagined snack maker redesigns its packets. This change comes from the
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** legal environment. Laws, rules and regulations that a business must follow make up the legal environment.

questions.stem_md: Which one of the following is **not** a part of the macro environment of a business?

options.text_md: The prices charged by a rival in the same market
The rate of inflation in the economy
The literacy rate of the population
A new law on the privacy of customer data

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The prices charged by a rival in the same market. A rival's prices belong to the micro environment (competitors). Inflation (economic), literacy (social) and a privacy law (legal) are macro forces.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Growing health awareness has increased the demand for millet-based foods.

**Reason (R):** The social environment includes changes in people's values, habits and lifestyles.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and the reason explains the assertion: health awareness is a social change that alters what people buy.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Online shopping apps have changed the way many small retailers sell.

**Reason (R):** The political environment includes the stability of the government.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true, but government stability (political) does not explain the change in retailing, which is technological.

questions.stem_md: A change in the tastes and preferences of consumers is part of the technological environment.
questions.solution_md: **False.** False. Tastes and preferences belong to the social environment.

questions.stem_md: Interest rates, inflation and per capita income are factors of the ___ environment.
questions.solution_md: They are economic factors.

questions.stem_md: Match each change faced by an imagined travel agency with the macro dimension it belongs to.

options.text_md: More families now take short weekend trips
Customers book tickets through a new AI travel app
A new rule caps cancellation fees on air tickets
Rising fuel prices push up air fares

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(q), (b)–(s), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). Travel habits are social; apps are technological; a rule on fees is legal; fuel prices and fares are economic.

questions.stem_md: Explain how each of the following changes could affect an imagined two-wheeler showroom: (i) banks raise interest rates on vehicle loans; (ii) more young buyers prefer electric scooters.
questions.solution_md: Each change linked to its dimension and its effect.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Economic environment:** costlier loans **reduce demand**, since many buyers purchase on credit.
(ii) **Social environment:** the showroom must **stock electric models** and train staff, or lose young buyers.

questions.stem_md: Malwa Bakes (imagined), Indore, faces three changes: a new labelling law, a rise in wheat prices, and customers choosing whole-grain bread. Identify the macro dimension of each change and explain one effect on the bakery.
questions.solution_md: Each change classified and its effect explained.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Labelling law — legal:** packs must be **redesigned** to show the required details, adding cost.
2. **Rising wheat prices — economic:** **raw-material cost** rises, squeezing margins or forcing a price increase.
3. **Whole-grain preference — social:** the bakery should **add whole-grain lines** to keep customers.

questions.stem_md: Explain liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation as changes in the economic environment of Indian business since 1991.
questions.solution_md: Each of the three changes explained.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Liberalisation:** removal of unnecessary **controls and licences**, freeing firms to decide on production, prices and expansion.
2. **Privatisation:** a **reduced role of the public sector**, with government sharing or selling ownership of public enterprises.
3. **Globalisation:** **integration** of the Indian economy with the world economy through freer **trade, investment and technology** flows.

questions.stem_md: Explain the five components of the macro environment, giving for each an example of a change that could affect an imagined mobile-accessories shop.
questions.solution_md: One mark for each component with a suitable example.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Economic:** interest rates, inflation, incomes and policies — a **fall in incomes** reduces spending on accessories.
2. **Social:** values, habits, demographics — more **students using phones for study** raises demand for chargers.
3. **Technological:** new methods and products — a new **charging standard** makes old cables obsolete.
4. **Political:** stability and government attitude — **stable policies** encourage the shop to invest in a second outlet.
5. **Legal:** laws and rules — a rule on **safety certification** of chargers forces it to stock certified items.

questions.stem_md: In a SWOT analysis, which two elements come from the firm's **internal** environment?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Strengths and weaknesses. Strengths and weaknesses are inside the firm; opportunities and threats come from the external environment.

questions.stem_md: An imagined bakery has three master bakers trained in France and a cake recipe that customers cannot find elsewhere. In its SWOT analysis, these are
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** strengths. Skilled staff and a unique recipe are internal advantages: strengths.

questions.stem_md: A large supermarket chain plans to open a store with a bakery section in the same market as the imagined bakery. In the bakery's SWOT analysis, this is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** a threat. An external development that could hurt the bakery is a threat.

questions.stem_md: A state government announces subsidies for small food-processing units that buy energy-efficient ovens. For a small imagined bakery, this is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** an opportunity. A favourable external development the firm can use is an opportunity.

questions.stem_md: Zari Threads (imagined) has outdated machines, no website and depends on a single buyer for most of its sales. In SWOT terms these are
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** weaknesses. Internal limitations of the firm are weaknesses. (Dependence on one buyer is an internal weakness of its sales base, even though the buyer is outside.)

questions.stem_md: In a SWOT analysis, opportunities and threats arise from the external environment of the firm.
questions.solution_md: **True.** True. Opportunities and threats come from changes outside the firm, such as new rivals or new government schemes; strengths and weaknesses lie inside it.

questions.stem_md: What is SWOT analysis? Why is it useful to a small business?
questions.solution_md: Meaning with all four elements, plus usefulness.

answer.model_answer_md: **SWOT analysis** is a study of a firm's internal **Strengths** and **Weaknesses** and the external **Opportunities** and **Threats** it faces. It helps a small business **build on strengths, correct weaknesses, use opportunities and guard against threats** when planning.

questions.stem_md: Prepare a simple SWOT analysis for Tamarind Tiffins (imagined), a home-food lunch service in Madurai, using these facts: loyal office customers; only two delivery staff; offices returning to full attendance; cloud kitchens opening nearby.
questions.solution_md: Each fact placed correctly in S, W, O or T with a short reason.

answer.model_answer_md:
| | |
|---|---|
| **Strength:** loyal office customers who trust home-style food | **Weakness:** only two delivery staff limit growth and speed |
| **Opportunity:** offices returning to **full attendance** mean more lunch orders | **Threat:** **cloud kitchens** nearby compete on variety and app ordering |

questions.stem_md:
Kosi Cane Crafts is an imagined cane-furniture unit in Purnea run by eight artisans. It has a strong local reputation and low costs, but no website and little working capital. Hotel chains are looking for eco-friendly furniture, while cheap plastic furniture is flooding the market and a new rule requires fire-safety labels on furniture for hotels.
(a) Prepare a SWOT analysis for the unit. [4]
(b) Suggest one strategy that uses a strength to grab an opportunity. [1]
questions.solution_md: Each element correctly classified (the labelling rule is an external threat or, if met, an advantage); a strategy matching a strength to an opportunity.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Strengths** (internal, helpful): a strong **local reputation** built over years, and **low costs**, because eight skilled artisans work with locally grown cane.
**Weaknesses** (internal, harmful): **no website**, so distant buyers cannot find the unit; and **little working capital**, so it cannot buy material in advance for large orders.
**Opportunities** (external, helpful): **hotel chains** looking for **eco-friendly** furniture, a growing and well-paying market.
**Threats** (external, harmful): **cheap plastic furniture** flooding the market; and the new **fire-safety labelling rule**, which adds cost and paperwork if the unit cannot comply.

(b) Use its **low costs and reputation** to offer **certified, eco-friendly cane sets** to hotel chains. By meeting the labelling rule, it turns the rule into a selling point rather than a barrier.

answer.model_answer_md:

questions.passage_md:
**Brahmaputra Boatworks (imagined), Guwahati**

Brahmaputra Boatworks builds fibreglass ferries. Every Friday its manager, Rituparna, spends an hour reading river-transport news, talking to boat operators and checking the rates of two rival yards. Last month she learnt that the state plans to add twenty new ferry routes, and that the resin supplier in Kolkata may raise prices. The boatworks also depends on a cooperative bank for working capital and on a trucking firm to carry boats to the river.

children.stem_md: Rituparna's Friday routine is an example of
children.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** environmental scanning. Regularly gathering and analysing information about the environment is environmental scanning.

children.stem_md: Name the external micro factor represented by the resin supplier.
children.solution_md: The resin supplier provides raw material: a supplier.

answer.model_answer_md: **Suppliers.**

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): Identify two other external micro factors in the passage and explain how each matters to the boatworks.
children.solution_md: Two factors from the passage with their importance.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Financier:** the **cooperative bank** provides working capital; its terms affect how many boats can be built.
2. **Marketing intermediary / competitors:** the **trucking firm** decides timely delivery; the **two rival yards** set price limits.

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): Classify the twenty new ferry routes and the possible resin price rise as opportunities or threats, with reasons.

answer.model_answer_md:
**New ferry routes — opportunity:** more routes mean **more orders** for ferries.
**Resin price rise — threat:** higher **raw-material cost** may cut margins or force price increases.

questions.stem_md: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow. *(Imagined firm, written by SOYL for practice.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** **Correct option: (d)** Legal. Rules a business must follow form the legal environment.

**(b)** The line about the delivery app.

**(c) (i)** One internal strength and one internal weakness.

**OR (c) (ii)** Links the economic change to fixing the weakness.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (d) Legal

**(b)** "**a delivery app has made it easy for cafés to order supplies online**".

**(c) (i)** **Strength:** **highly skilled chefs**. **Weakness:** a **small cold-storage unit**, which limits how much it can stock.

**OR (c) (ii)** Cheaper **loans (economic opportunity)** let the firm **borrow to enlarge its cold storage**, removing the weakness that limits its stock and sales.

questions.passage_md:

Kalimpong Kitchens makes ready-to-eat momos and sells them through cafés. Its chefs are highly skilled, but its cold-storage unit is small. Recently, more young people have started eating packaged snacks at work, a new food-safety rule requires a licence number on every pack, banks have cut interest rates on small business loans, and a delivery app has made it easy for cafés to order supplies online.

children.stem_md: The new food-safety rule belongs to which dimension of the macro environment?
children.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Legal. Rules a business must follow form the legal environment.

children.stem_md: Quote the line that shows a change in the technological environment.

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): Identify one strength and one weakness of the firm from the passage.

answer.model_answer_md: **Strength:** **highly skilled chefs**. **Weakness:** a **small cold-storage unit**, which limits how much it can stock.
